common_name: UFBeauty Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; UFBeauty requires only about 250–300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any peach cultivar, making it well suited to the mild winters of zone 9 and coastal Gulf gardens.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first year to establish good light penetration and easy harvest access. UFBeauty is a University of Florida release from the same low-chill peach breeding program that produced Flordaking and TropicBeauty, bred specifically to bloom and fruit reliably where standard peach varieties fail to accumulate enough winter chill, ripening medium-large, attractive red-blushed yellow freestone fruit of good quality in late spring. Its very low chill requirement makes it one of the most dependable peach choices for the warmest parts of zone 9, where many older peach cultivars bloom too early, too late, or too erratically to set a reliable crop. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart when marble-sized to improve size and quality, and provide full sun and sharp drainage, since peach roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet soil.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — low-chill peach variety development
LSU AgCenter — Low-Chill Peach Variety Recommendations for the Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Peach Variety Selection for Texas and the Gulf Coast

common_name: Gulf King Peach (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; Gulf King is part of a family of low-chill 'Gulf' series peaches bred for the Gulf Coast, requiring only around 350 chill hours to bloom and fruit reliably in mild winters.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and thin developing fruit to 6–8 inches apart once they reach marble size to improve final fruit quality. Gulf King is one of a series of low-chill peach cultivars bred for Gulf Coast growing conditions, sharing the Gulf-series naming with siblings like Gulfprince and Gulfcrest, producing medium to large, firm, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with attractive red-blushed skin in early to mid season. Its moderate-low chill requirement provides reliable bloom and fruit set through the region's variable, often too-warm winters, giving Gulf South gardeners a dependable option among the several regionally bred low-chill peach releases. Prune annually to an open-vase form for good light penetration, and protect the shallow, rot-prone root system with sharply drained soil.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Peach Variety Selection for Texas and the Gulf Coast
LSU AgCenter — Low-Chill Peach Variety Recommendations for the Gulf South

common_name: Necta Zee Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Container Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Necta Zee is a genetic dwarf reaching only 5–6 feet tall, making it one of the few stone fruit trees well suited to large containers or very small garden spaces.

directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, in the ground or in a large container of at least 15–20 gallons, and thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart when marble-sized, since the naturally dwarf, densely fruiting tree can easily overset relative to its small size. Necta Zee is a genetic dwarf nectarine, naturally compact rather than grafted onto dwarfing rootstock, reaching only about 5–6 feet tall with a dense, bushy habit, yet still producing full-sized, sweet, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with the classic smooth nectarine skin in mid-summer. Its true dwarf stature makes it one of the very few stone fruits practical for a patio container, small urban yard, or anywhere a full-sized 15–20 foot peach or nectarine tree would be impractical, while requiring the same full sun, sharp drainage, and moderate chill (around 500 hours) as standard nectarine varieties. Prune lightly to maintain an open center for light and air circulation, and watch for the leaf curl and brown rot diseases common to nectarines in humid climates.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — genetic dwarf stone fruit variety notes

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Theta requires a compatible pollinator cultivar with overlapping bloom time nearby, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinator cultivar planted within about 50–60 feet for reliable cross-pollination, since hazelnuts require wind transfer of pollen between genetically compatible trees. Theta was developed by Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program and released with strong resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that has devastated susceptible hazelnut orchards, allowing more reliable production without the intensive disease management older, susceptible cultivars require. It produces medium to large, well-filled, high-quality nuts on a vigorous, productive tree, harvested in early fall as they naturally drop from the husk. Hazelnuts perform best in regions with cool, humid growing seasons and moderate winter chill, making them a better fit for the upper South and Pacific Northwest-like climates than the hot, humid Deep South, where summer heat and disease pressure limit success. Rake and collect fallen nuts promptly to prevent rodent loss and mold.
sources: Oregon State University — hazelnut breeding program release notes
Oregon State University Extension — Eastern filbert blight resistance trials

common_name: Bouche de Betizac Chestnut (Large-Nutted Blight-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Bouche de Betizac benefits from a compatible pollinator chestnut nearby for the best nut set, though it shows some self-fertility.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator chestnut within range for the best nut production, since yields improve substantially with cross-pollination even in partially self-fertile cultivars. Bouche de Betizac is a French-bred hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut species, combining the large, sweet, high-quality nuts prized in European chestnut cookery with meaningful resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that devastated native American chestnut populations and continues to threaten susceptible European chestnut plantings. It bears precociously, often producing a first crop within just a few years of planting, and continues with heavy, reliable yields of large, easy-to-peel nuts on a vigorous, productive tree. Its blight resistance and large nut size have made it a popular choice for both commercial and home chestnut orchards seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant alternative to susceptible pure European chestnut cultivars. Harvest nuts as burs split and drop in fall, collecting promptly to avoid rodent and insect loss.
sources: Chestnut Growers of America — hybrid chestnut cultivar records
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — chestnut cultivar trials
